This annual report, which covers the period from July 1, 2025, to 
June 30, 2026, has been prepared by the World Bank Group Boards 
of Directors. Ajay Banga, President of the World Bank Group and 
Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, has submitted this 
report, together with the accompanying administrative budgets and 
audited financial statements, to the Board of Governors. All dollar amounts used in this report are current U.S. dollars unless 
otherwise specified. As a result of rounding, numbers in tables may 
not add to totals, and percentages in figures may not add to 100.

Each institution — ICSID, IFC, MIGA, and the World Bank (IBRD/IDA) —  
has also prepared a separate report with its own fiscal 2026 financial 
data. To download these reports, visit: https://www.worldbank.org/en/

To achieve this, we are working with all clients as One World Bank Group, 
in close partnership with other multilateral institutions, the private sector, 
and civil society. The World Bank Group includes:
• International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), 
which provides financial products and policy advice to help countries reduce 
poverty and extend the benefits of sustainable growth to all their people. • International Development Association (IDA), 
which provides grants and concessional loans to low-income countries.

• International Finance Corporation (IFC), 
which mobilizes private capital at scale, supports businesses from 
microenterprises to large corporations, and creates jobs that drive economic 
growth and opportunity. • Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), 
which houses the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform, providing 
guarantees to mobilize private capital for developing countries. • International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), 
which provides international facilities for conciliation, mediation, and 
arbitration of investment disputes.

Our mission is to end extreme poverty and boost 
shared prosperity on a livable planet. This mission is 
threatened by multiple, intertwined crises. Time is of the 
essence. Through the Knowledge Bank and our financial 
commitments, we are driving impactful development 
that is:
• Inclusive of everyone, including women and young people. • Resilient to shocks and fragility. • Sustainable, through growth and job creation, human development, 
fiscal and debt management, food security, and access to clean air, water, 
and affordable energy.

The World Bank Group Guarantee Platform, 
hosted at MIGA, continues to play a vital role in 
bringing private capital to emerging markets. The Board commends MIGA for surpassing 
$100 billion in cumulative guarantee issuance 
since its founding in 1988, a remarkable 
achievement from just $366 million in paid-in 
capital. In addition, in fiscal 2026, the World Bank 
Group surpassed its goal of $20 billion in annual 
guarantee issuance — four years ahead of the 
2030 target.

The Board endorsed the extension of the World 
Bank Group’s Climate Change Action Plan, a 
significant step that provides vital continuity for 
countries. The Executive Directors expect the 
institution to be measured by the tangible impact 
its work has on communities worldwide, and the 
Board is grateful for the strong collaboration with 
Management on this initiative. Throughout the year, the Board actively engaged 
with government counterparts, World Bank Group 
staff, development partners, beneficiaries, civil 
society organizations, and private sector entities.

Delegations of Executive Directors and Alternate 
Executive Directors undertook five official 
trips, including visits to West and Central Africa 
(Sierra Leone and Chad), Latin America and the 
Caribbean (Dominican Republic, and St. Vincent 
and the Grenadines), and the Middle East and 
North Africa (Algeria and Lebanon).

Additionally, 
delegations conducted two thematic trips: to 
Portugal and Cabo Verde to study the energy 
transition and sustainable use of marine resources 
in fostering growth in coastal areas, and to Chile 
and Argentina, focusing on advancing the energy 
transition while strengthening water security. These visits provided invaluable, first-hand insights 
into country priorities and on-the-ground results, 
while strengthening connections with clients and 
the growing number of staff located in the field.

Looking ahead, the Executive Directors and 
Management share a unified, ambitious vision 
anchored in a clear set of priorities: delivering on 
the jobs strategy, disseminating knowledge and 
expertise through the Knowledge Bank, scaling 
private capital mobilization, and strengthening 
operational effectiveness in fragile and conflict-
affected settings.

While sustained progress 
ultimately depends on strong country ownership 
and close collaboration with partners across the 
international development system, the Board 
works hand-in-hand with Management to ensure 
the institution pulls every lever at its disposal. Together, the Board and Management are 
committed to realizing a more resilient future —  
one where economic growth creates jobs that 
deliver dignity, hope, and lasting opportunity.

The Board extends its sincere gratitude to the 
World Bank Group President, Management, and 
staff whose tireless efforts are instrumental in 
advancing these goals, ensuring that progress is 
transformative and far-reaching. The Executive Directors support the World Bank 
Group’s urgent response to these crises while 
maintaining a resolute focus on the long-term 
challenge of creating jobs at scale. The Board is 
encouraged that countries can increasingly access 
fast-acting finance for emergency response, 
with 79 countries to date utilizing Crisis Toolkit 
Arrangements.

In fiscal 2026, the Board reaffirmed 
its support for the World Bank Group’s strategic 
drive to create more and better-paid jobs as total 
World Bank Group commitments for the year 
reached $123.5 billion.1
The Board welcomes the World Bank Group’s 
new ways of working. By deepening collaboration 
across our institutions, we are enhancing 
efficiency and accelerating our impact on the 
ground.

Forging new alliances with private 
sector partners and clients and strengthening 
cooperation with development partners ensures 
that scarce resources are deployed where they can 
generate the most jobs and growth. Furthermore, 
the Executive Directors recognize the critical 
role of the Knowledge Bank — harnessing the 
institution’s data, analytics, and operational 
experience — in delivering more impactful, 
country-led projects. The Board was also pleased 
this year to approve the creation of a single, 
independent accountability mechanism, informed 
by extensive consultations.

JOBS ARE ESSENTIAL. THEY 
PROVIDE DIGNITY, HOPE, AND 
BELIEF IN A BETTER FUTURE. When jobs are created at scale, they strengthen communities, transform countries, and 
power the global economy. Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in developing 
countries. Those countries are expected to create only about 420 million jobs.

Whether this 
generation becomes an engine of growth or a source of instability will depend in large part on 
whether they can find productive work. That is why creating jobs is the overarching focus of the World Bank Group. Three years ago, our shareholders and clients gave us a clear mandate: build a better and 
bigger World Bank Group — faster, simpler, and better able to bring private capital alongside 
our own financing and knowledge. We changed how we work. We shortened average project preparation and approval times 
from 19 months to nine.

We brought the institutions of the World Bank Group together 
around countries and clients — anchored in one country strategy built around each country’s 
needs and development priorities. We created a single platform for guarantees, simplified our 
products and internal structures, developed a purposeful work plan to support the private 
sector in emerging markets, and replaced a scorecard of 153 indicators with 22 measures 
focused on results. And we began building vehicles that can connect development projects 
with investors managing capital at real scale.

can meet the jobs challenge alone. But this 
year demonstrated what is possible when our

The World Bank Group is faster, simpler, and 
better equipped to deliver. Now we must build 
on that progress — and help create more jobs for 
more people. These changes matter because public resources 
alone cannot meet the need. Our financing 
and knowledge can help countries build the 
foundations for growth and create the conditions 
for investment. But creating jobs at scale requires 
private businesses. The private sector accounts 
for 90 percent of jobs globally, the vast majority of 
them through small- and medium-sized businesses, 
and entrepreneurs.

This year’s results show the progress we have 
made. We delivered $123.5 billion in financing 
to clients. We mobilized $112 billion in private 
capital, more than triple the $35 billion we 
mobilized in fiscal 2022. Altogether, that brought 
our total financing and mobilization in developing 
economies to well over $200 billion in fiscal 2026. The growth was broad-based.

Between fiscal 2022 
and fiscal 2026, private capital mobilization nearly 
tripled in lower-middle-income countries, from 
$14 billion to $37 billion; more than quadrupled in 
upper-middle-income countries, from $12 billion 
to $50 billion; and increased by nearly 150 percent 
across Africa, from $9 billion to $22 billion.

In low-income countries, where private 
investment is hardest to attract, we deployed 
our own financing to support development 
priorities — and mobilized roughly $3 billion 
in private capital alongside it, extending the 
reach of our resources and our ability to meet 
the need in places affected by fragility, conflict, 
and violence. In short, as we support countries 
to grow and develop, private capital supplants 
public capital in driving jobs and growth.

Overall, more than half of the capital mobilized 
went to the sectors with the greatest potential to

REFORMS 
AND RESULTS
Three years ago, the World Bank Group launched its reform agenda 
with a clear ambition: to become a faster, simpler, more effective, 
and impactful institution — one better equipped to meet the scale and 
urgency of today’s development challenges. That agenda is now delivering results:
• Private capital mobilization 
Public capital alone is not enough to tackle the world’s most pressing 
development challenges.

That’s why we mobilized $112 billion in private 
funds in fiscal 2026 — more than triple the $35 billion mobilized in fiscal 
2022 — to further expand opportunity, create jobs, and build infrastructure. We also issued $25 billion in guarantees this year — surpassing our goal of 
issuing $20 billion annually by 2030 — to give investors the confidence to 
invest in developing countries.

• MDB partnerships 
The Global Collaborative Co-Financing Platform, of which we are a founding 
member, has a pipeline of almost 240 projects valued at $140 billion, and we’ve 
removed co-financing fees to spur even more partnerships. We’ve also agreed to 
Full Mutual Reliance Frameworks with two multilateral development banks that 
allow clients to engage with a single lead lender and their operational policies. • Knowledge transfer 
We’re applying our data and insights to better help clients create jobs.

Assessments such as The Global Jobs Challenge map constraints, reforms, and 
investment opportunities. The World Bank Group Academy continues to build 
client capacity with practical, tested development solutions. • Greater efficiency 
Across the World Bank Group, we’ve consolidated country office leadership 
and eliminated bureaucratic duplication, making it faster and easier for us to 
address our clients’ priorities. We cut average project-approval times from 
19 months to nine, with some low-risk projects approved in as little as 60 days.

• Corporate initiatives 
We’re deploying AI to accelerate our work and working with partners to promote 
AI solutions that are safe and impactful for everyone. We focus on practical 
applications that solve everyday problems in developing countries. • Clear outcomes 
Our Scorecard now focuses on 22 key metrics that show how our work creates 
jobs and improves lives. And our Target Map keeps us ambitious against 10 
strategic priorities. We publish our data online, making it more user-friendly and 
leading to better outcomes.

Jobs unlock potential, empower women, engage young people, 
strengthen communities, create business opportunities and support 
entrepreneurs, and reduce dependence on development assistance. Giving people the means to move up the ladder of aspirations lifts 
entire communities out of poverty.

When we create jobs, we strengthen economic and social stability, 
reduce mass migration, improve livelihoods, enhance resilience to 
economic shocks, and prevent people from falling back into poverty. That benefits everyone, everywhere. With 1.2 billion young people reaching working age in the next 10 to 
15 years, the need for more and better-paid jobs is more urgent than 
ever. On current trajectories, developing countries are expected to 
generate only about 420 million jobs over that same period — leaving a 
gap of staggering proportions.

Jobs are created when firms can operate reliably, plan with confidence, 
and invest with reasonable expectations of return. Our strategy reflects 
that reality:
• First, invest in foundational physical and human infrastructure;
• Second, support a business-enabling environment with clear rules 
and regulations;
• And third, mobilize private capital at scale. The Knowledge Bank plays a crucial role, bringing decades of frontline 
experience to provide insight into the reforms that have helped 
countries and companies thrive.

To multiply our impact, we’re mobilizing affordable, concessional 
finance through IDA, and private capital through IFC, MIGA, and the 
World Bank (IBRD/IDA). But development at scale requires an orchestra — governments, 
development institutions, philanthropists, and private investors 
all working in concert. With bold action and a shared commitment, we can turn the promise 
of future generations into jobs, dignity, and prosperity. JOBS STRATEGY
The world needs more and better-paid 
jobs, and it needs them fast.

Water security is foundational for productivity and economic growth. As one 
of the most water-scarce countries in the world, Jordan has struggled to grow 
its economy and create jobs for its young people. The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by 
initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water 
Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected 
to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply.

The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly, 
approximately 29,000 jobs, as well as advancing long-term job creation. The World Bank Group is part of a pool of international lenders providing 
financing for the project: In fiscal 2026, the Board approved an IFC loan of 
up to $375 million. IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million 
concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green 
Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of 
up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan 
Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This 
is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water 
reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness. The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our 
Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments, 
long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water 
security, economic growth, and job creation.

Attacks to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have created an estimated $91 billion 
in reconstruction needs. The World Bank Group is supporting the Government of 
Ukraine to develop a European Union (EU)-aligned energy sector strategy to restore 
security of supply, reestablish financial viability, mobilize private capital at scale, 
strengthen corporate governance of state energy companies, and improve financial 
sustainability — essential ingredients for economic competitiveness, productivity, and 
employment creation.

The World Bank Group is also offering Ukraine comprehensive financial and technical 
support. Re-PoWER, a World Bank trust fund-financed project, secured $403 million in 
grants to restore electricity and heating for millions of people. In fiscal 2026, more than 
$150 million of these grants were allocated for heating units, as well as for equipment 
needed to secure power imports from the EU. Another project is rehabilitating 
hydropower plants and delivering reliable power to affected communities.

In close coordination, IFC’s €50 million financing and support from partners unlocked 
the private investment to build a new 189 megawatt (MW) wind power plant by the 
Ukrainian company OKKO, complementing an earlier 147 MW project. The two projects 
are expected to contribute to Ukraine’s energy grid stability and provide electricity to 
around 800,000 people. Together with additional renewable energy projects supported by 
IFC and partners, these private sector investments are expected to add approximately 
715 MW of new capacity.
The World Bank Group is also promoting private sector resilience in Ukraine.

IBRD is 
supporting policy reforms across several economic sectors and helping to keep basic 
services for firms and citizens, while IFC has established risk-sharing facilities with 
Ukrainian financial institutions to support on-lending to micro, small, and medium 
enterprises; mobilized private sector participation in infrastructure, including telecom 
and energy; supported businesses to safeguard jobs and food security; and backed 
innovation and high-tech ventures through venture capital and private equity funds 
to retain talent and build future growth.

For its part, MIGA has extended and increased 
guarantees to free up capital linked to two banks’ mandatory reserves, issuing 
$448 million in new guarantees since February 2022 to keep small businesses 
afloat and maintain employment opportunities. REBUILDING

Brazil’s family farms employ nearly 10 million people and play a central 
role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched 
in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved 
technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030. This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority 
that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus. Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique 
capabilities.

First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations 
of family farms by investing in physical and human capital, such as rural 
roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards, 
repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. Finally, 
the World Bank Group expands access to finance through MIGA’s 
guarantees and insurance, as well as partnerships created by the 
World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across 
all three pillars.

With this approach, we’ll create an integrated pathway for family 
farms to access markets, finance, technology, and resilience tools. We’re working quickly because family farms around the world, including 
500 million smallholder farmers, produce most of the world’s food, 
yet many remain in poverty, relying on traditional farming methods 
and lacking access to markets, finance, and technology. Supporting 
them to become commercially successful is critical to creating jobs, 
reducing poverty, and improving global food security.

Pacific Island countries face some of the world’s highest rates of premature death and 
disability from non-communicable disease, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, 
and cancer, alongside persistent communicable diseases. Local healthcare systems 
struggle to provide care to dispersed populations, and the resulting inefficiencies drive 
up service costs and hamper job creation and long-term growth. The World Bank’s Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation (PHIT) project, approved in 
fiscal 2026, is taking a new approach to improving the health of people across the 
region.

The $239.5 million project covers Fiji, Kiribati, Tonga, and Tuvalu, and — through 
the Pacific Community — Naoero, Samoa, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu. Leveraging the expertise of Knowledge Bank teams at the World Bank and IFC, PHIT will 
create, protect, and safeguard 16,000 vital health and health-support jobs across the 
Pacific — spanning frontline service delivery, infrastructure development, digital health 
systems, supply chains, and monitoring and evaluation — representing a major 
investment in the region’s most critical asset: its people.

AI-enabled diagnostics and 
regional telehealth networks will enable more patients to receive accurate diagnostics; 
expanded access to specialized services, including regional radiotherapy and advanced 
medical imaging, will serve patients with specific needs. Together, these advancements 
will accelerate regional health and development impact for greater resilience, 
productivity, and inclusive growth.

PHIT is the largest World Bank Group multi-country operation in the Pacific and 
supports our strategic priority of delivering quality, affordable health services to 
1.5 billion people by 2030. It is also the first project developed with the Asian 
Development Bank under the Full Mutual Reliance Framework, helping reduce 
transaction costs. The OPEC Fund and the Pandemic Fund are also co-financing 
PHIT, which is set to help Pacific Island countries establish the fundamental 
conditions for good health, jobs, and growth.

Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a 
quarter of GDP. But for years, the sector has been constrained by a narrow 
model dominated by all-inclusive resorts in only two of the archipelago’s 
10 islands, with few links to local businesses. Infrastructure deficits, a 
shortage of skilled hospitality workers, and the absence of a coherent 
framework for attracting quality investment left the country exposed and 
its potential unrealized.

The World Bank Group has worked across its private and public sector 
arms to help Cabo Verde chart a more diversified and inclusive tourism 
sector. Two World Bank operations — the Resilient Tourism and Blue 
Economy Development Project and the Improving Connectivity and Urban 
Infrastructure Project — are strengthening the sector’s governance and 
institutional framework, while upgrading critical infrastructure, including 
coastal and jetty facilities, maritime passenger terminals, heritage sites, 
and public spaces.

Two other programs — the Human Capital Development Project and the 
Health Security Program in Western and Central Africa — are complementing 
these efforts by strengthening essential services. Together they support 
more than 100 vocational and specialty training courses, translating growth 
into more and better-paid jobs. IFC has anchored the private sector transformation. In December 2023, 
IFC arranged a financing package of up to €35.5 million for Oásis Atlântico, 
one of the country’s leading hospitality operators.

The investment supports 
more than 700 direct jobs and 20,000 indirect jobs, and linkages with over 
700 small suppliers and farmers. IFC has also extended two successive 
sustainability-linked loans to Cabo Verde Airports S.A., a subsidiary of VINCI 
Airports, with the most recent reaching up to €60 million in February 2026. The financing has modernized and greened the country’s seven airports, 
created over 2,000 direct jobs and 1,200 indirect jobs, and helped establish 
35 new air routes — driving a 60 percent surge in passenger volumes 
since 2022.

The results are reshaping Cabo Verde’s tourism landscape. Average daily 
tourist spending and overnight stays in previously under-visited islands 
are both rising, and growing private investment signals confidence in the 
country’s trajectory. With the World Bank Group supporting the full arc from 
governance and infrastructure to skills and private finance, Cabo Verde is 
building a more diversified, sustainable, and job-rich tourism economy.

India aspires to become an upper-middle-income economy in the next 
decade. Its National Green Hydrogen Mission, which aims to catalyze 
600,000 jobs by 2030, is critical to meeting this goal. Since 2021, the World Bank Group has helped India advance 
hydrogen hub planning, enabling infrastructure, and public-private 
engagement to mobilize private sector investment. In fiscal 2026, IFC 
invested $25 million in Hygenco Green Energies — its first direct green 
hydrogen investment in India.

This investment is complemented by 
two IFC-managed blended finance facilities, the Clean Technology 
Fund ($20 million) and the Frontier Opportunities Fund ($5 million), 
which altogether enabled $55 million in co-investment from other 
private sector partners. The total financing package, including equity from other partners, will 
support the creation of more than 1,000 direct and indirect jobs across 
the green hydrogen value chain and broader industrial ecosystem over

BUSINESS OVERVIEW 
PRIVATE CAPITAL MOBILIZATION 
AND JOBS 
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale 
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of 
finance to a platform that channels global capital 
flows into developing countries. Rather than 
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are 
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and 
our convening role to crowd private capital into the 
most productive sectors for job creation.

This means 
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms 
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader 
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool 
of global capital to development opportunities. In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that 
are already translating into results. While financing 
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from 
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years, 
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in 
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

This more than 
threefold increase represents a fundamental shift in 
our ability to bring external capital into development 
opportunities at scale, making us the largest mobilizer 
of private capital among multilateral development 
banks. Guarantees issued by the World Bank Group 
Guarantee Platform grew by 46 percent in fiscal 
2026. We are providing patient equity in markets 
where early-stage capital is scarce and expanding 
local-currency financing where foreign-exchange risk 
would otherwise deter investment.

We also began 
piloting “originate-to-distribute” approaches to connect 
institutional investors with emerging market assets at 
greater scale. And we’re providing investors and ratings 
agencies with historical data on the performance 
of emerging market lending through the Global 
Emerging Markets Risk Database. These practical 
shifts are already supporting investment and jobs. A NEW APPROACH TO 
COUNTRY ENGAGEMENT 
We are building a One World Bank Group client 
coverage model that aligns public and private sector 
solutions around jobs, growth, and private investment.

Our new approach is more efficient, outcome-focused, 
and systematic in tapping private sector solutions 
and will help countries tackle their development 
challenges with greater speed, quality, and impact. The centerpiece of this new approach is our 
Country Partnership Framework (CPF) — the 
key tool that guides our strategic engagement 
with countries. CPFs typically span four to six 
years, with a maximum duration of 10 years, to 
align our support with a country’s development 
goals and the World Bank Group Scorecard.

In fiscal 2026, we delivered 28 new CPFs that are 
underpinned by five core diagnostics: Country 
Climate and Development Reports, Country 
Growth and Jobs Reports, Country Private Sector 
Diagnostics, Poverty and Equity Assessments, and 
Public Finance Reviews. From this data, we identify 
three to five outcomes that support job creation, 
and complementary public and private actions to 
support the outcomes.

With outcomes defined at the 
intersection of three selectivity criteria — development 
challenges, country development goals, and World 
Bank Group comparative advantages — CPFs 
serve as the primary vehicle for translating World 
Bank Group targets and strategies into country-
level action, delivering on client priorities through 
complementary public and private solutions. We also conducted our first cross-World Bank 
Group business planning exercise in fiscal 2026.

We intend to make this an annual event so we can 
better respond to government needs and adapt 
our programs to evolving country contexts. 33

SUPPORT TO SMALL STATES 
Small states4 face distinct challenges, including 
remoteness, heavy import dependence, narrow 
economic bases, and high exposure to external shocks. The World Bank Group is expanding its resources to 
help small states address these challenges. In fiscal 
2026, IBRD/IDA portfolio net commitments to small 
states reached $8.9 billion, IFC portfolio exposure 
reached $682 million, and MIGA exposure reached 
$790 million. We are also intensifying our focus on climate 
adaptation for small states.

As of June 30, 2026, 
30 small states have signed on to at least one 
arrangement from the Crisis Preparedness and 
Response Toolkit. In fiscal 2026, we published Country 
Climate and Development Reports for Botswana, 
Gabon, The Gambia, Mauritius, Namibia, and 
Seychelles. We are preparing reports for seven more 
small states — Barbados, Belize, Equatorial Guinea, 
Fiji, São Tomé and Príncipe, Solomon Islands, and 
Timor-Leste — to be published within the next two 
fiscal years. During the Spring Meetings in April 2026, the 
World Bank Group launched the Small States 
Strategy.

Guided by select solutions underpinned 
by the World Bank Group Jobs Framework, the Strategy 
prioritizes interventions with the greatest potential 
to support job creation and economic growth. Support will be differentiated to reflect individual 
country contexts, while using regional approaches, 
aggregated procurement, capacity building, and 
stronger partnerships to address scale constraints, 
high transaction costs, and partner fragmentation. Implementation is anchored in Country Partnership 
Frameworks.

The Strategy was informed by feedback 
from small states gathered through consultations 
and engagement, including at the annual Small States 
Forum held alongside the World Bank Group Annual 
Meetings in October 2025. For more information, visit https://www. worldbank.org/en/country/smallstates. SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 
IN CAPITAL MARKETS 
IBRD has mobilized finance for middle-income 
countries for more than 75 years, raising over 
$1 trillion from capital markets since issuing its first 
bond in 1947.

triple-A by the major credit rating agencies, raised 
nearly $50 billion through Sustainable Development 
Bonds issued in a variety of structures and maturities. Please see the IBRD’s annual Impact Report for more 
information about how funds raised in the capital 
markets support IBRD-financed projects. IDA also issues Sustainable Development Bonds

2026, following action by the United States (U.S.)

borrowing strategy with $2 billion and $4 billion issued

FINANCIAL INNOVATIONS TO 
MAXIMIZE DEVELOPMENT IMPACT 
Shareholder support for IBRD’s innovative financing 
instruments continued to grow in fiscal 2026, 
strengthening our capacity to scale lending and tackle 
global challenges. Singapore pledged funds to our 
hybrid capital instrument and New Zealand became 
the first shareholder to subscribe to our Enhanced 
Callable Capital instrument, bringing hybrid capital 
contributions to $1.2 billion.

Together, these new 
instruments demonstrate IBRD’s strong leveraging 
power, turning $1 into $6-10 of additional lending over 
time, and unlocking tens of billions for global impact. IBRD has continued to structure outcome bonds that mobilize private capital for 
specific development projects. For example, in December 2025, IBRD issued a 
$200 million principal-protected bond, the Clean Cooking Outcome Bond, that 
mobilized private capital to support the distribution and use of cleaner cooking 
stoves in Ghana.

This outcome bond provides investors with a coupon that includes 
a fixed guaranteed component, and a variable component linked to the sale of carbon 
credits generated from the use of the cookstoves. This is the first outcome bond 
linking investors’ financial return to the generation of Internationally Transferred 
Mitigation Outcomes, with the governments of Ghana and Switzerland authorizing 
the cleaner cooking projects supported by this bond.

In April 2026, IBRD priced a $120 million principal-protected Spekboom Restoration 
Outcome Bond to support large-scale ecosystem restoration and job creation in South 
Africa’s Eastern Cape province. The 14-year bond offers investors a return linked to 
the successful restoration of spekboom, a native plant with high carbon sequestration 
capacity. Under the structure, $25 million is provided as up-front financing for 
the project, which aims to restore about 50,000 hectares of land and to create an 
estimated 11,000 local jobs.

provide technical assistance and credit

recycling and boosts lending capacity 
over the long term.

In fiscal 2026, the World Bank Group enhanced its

structure by integrating E&S teams from the World

level, establishing a global World Bank Group E&S 
Policy and Operations department and a global World 
Bank Group E&S Risk department. The new structure 
provides a more robust system for proactive risk 
management and helps us deliver safeguards with 
greater clarity, speed, and credibility, while reinforcing 
our commitment to quality and accountability.

Under the new structure, the operational teams design 
and structure projects, ensuring that investments are 
planned and executed in line with our E&S policies 
and standards from beginning to end. This team 
reports to the Vice Presidents and Managing Directors 
for Operations. The second team institutionalizes a 
monitoring function. It reports to the Chief Risk Officer 
and ensures compliance over time, stepping in to take 
corrective action when needed. Crucially, the same 
people who design and execute a project are not the 
ones evaluating it afterward.

The Administrative Council is the governing body of 
ICSID. Its composition, functions, and decision-making 
procedures are outlined in the ICSID Convention 
(Articles 4 to 8).

The ICSID Administrative Council 
consists of one representative and one alternate 
representative from each Contracting State. Unless 
otherwise designated, the Governor for the World Bank 
appointed by that State serves as its representative on 
the ICSID Administrative Council. Each Contracting State has one vote on the Administrative 
Council, and there is no weighted voting on any matter. At the end of fiscal 2026, 158 Contracting States were 
represented on the ICSID Administrative Council.

The 
ICSID Administrative Council does not play a role in the 
administration of individual cases at ICSID. The President of the World Bank Group serves as the 
Chair of the Administrative Council (Article 5 of the ICSID 
Convention). The Chair does not have a vote on matters 
before the Administrative Council but is responsible for 
convening and presiding over its meetings. For more information, including an up-to-date 
list of members of the ICSID Administrative 
Council, visit https://icsid.worldbank.org/

TRUST FUNDS 
The World Bank Group manages a diverse portfolio of 
trust funds, which receive resources from more than 
100 donors. Trust funds are part of the World Bank 
Group’s toolkit and complement its core financing. They can mobilize funding quickly to fill financing gaps, 
offset risks, and provide flexibility. This often means the 
World Bank Group can work in the most challenging 
environments and deliver impact even where core 
financing is limited or unavailable. Trust funds broaden 
World Bank Group partnerships to more effectively 
address country, regional, and global challenges.

Trust funds also serve as force multipliers for the World 
Bank Group’s development impact, enabling IBRD to 
build public sector foundations, IFC to catalyze private 
investment, and MIGA to de-risk both. This integrated 
approach unlocks private investment and delivers 
results at scale by leveraging each institution’s unique 
strengths while working cohesively toward shared 
development objectives. While trust funds can vary in 
size and scope, they all serve the World Bank Group’s 
mission to end extreme poverty and boost shared 
prosperity on a livable planet.

The World Bank uses trust funds to strengthen the 
public sector foundations essential for development. At the end of fiscal 2026, World Bank trust funds 
held $27.9 billion in trust as cash, investments, and 
promissory notes. In the last five years (fiscal 2022–26), 
91 percent ($67.2 billion) of World Bank trust fund 
disbursements went to recipient-executed activities in 
member countries, helping to build the foundations 
for job growth including infrastructure, institutions, 
and human capital.

Of this amount, over $8.1 billion 
was disbursed to IDA and IDA-blend countries (i.e., 
countries eligible for both IDA and IBRD lending). Trust 
funds serve as engines of innovation, funding about 
two-thirds of the World Bank’s advisory services and 
analytics that lay the groundwork for both public and 
private investment. CATALYZING PRIVATE SECTOR INVESTMENT 
While the World Bank builds public sector foundations, 
IFC catalyzes private sector investment, mobilizing 
private capital with support from development 
partners.

In fiscal 2026, IFC deployed nearly 
$1.4 billion in partner funding across its blended 
finance, upstream, and advisory activities, helping 
transform markets, mobilize investment, and support 
job creation in challenging environments. This 
sustained donor support reflects the strength of IFC’s 
longstanding relationships with development partners. IFC’s blended finance trust funds provide concessional 
donor funding, combining it with IFC’s own-account 
financing to make high-impact projects viable in 
challenging markets.

On average, from fiscal 
2018–2026, every dollar of blended finance helped 
unlock more than $6 in total investment. Approximately 
41 percent of partner contributions to IFC blended 
finance trust funds signed in fiscal 2026 will support 
private sector development in fragile and conflict-
affected situations, demonstrating how trust funds 
enable IFC to operate where risks are highest and 
needs are greatest.

Tailored blended finance solutions, 
including several innovative approaches introduced 
or expanded during the year, helped advance projects 
that could not proceed on commercial terms alone. To support Ukraine’s private sector, IFC and the 
European Commission established the first High Impact 
Equity Guarantee Program for Ukraine to mobilize 
equity investment, including in infrastructure and 
small and medium enterprises, with strong potential 
for replication in other emerging markets.

Also in 
fiscal 2026, Italy joined eight other IFC development 
partners — Belgium, the European Commission, France, 
Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland, and 
the United Kingdom — to support IFC’s investment 
program in Ukraine, which helps sustain critical sectors 
and supports Ukraine’s reconstruction, including 
agribusiness, energy, and technology, and enables 
businesses to continue operating despite security risks, 
labor shortages, and rising input costs. IFC trust funds 
have now received more than $1 billion in concessional 
finance commitments for Ukraine.

The Catalytic First Loss Guarantee Program (CFLG) 
under IFC’s Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises 
(MSME) Finance Platform illustrates how close World 
Bank Group collaboration can expand financing for 
MSMEs, one of IFC’s key priorities. Supported by the 
IDA Private Sector Window trust fund, this program 
provides guarantees to private financial intermediaries.

In fiscal 2026, the program fully deployed its Board-
approved $20 million CFLG envelope trust fund 
allocation alongside $22 million of IFC own-account 
financing, together mobilizing $224 million in 
total financing — including $202 million in private 
capital — an 11-fold multiple of the trust fund allocation, 
and demonstrating the potential to further scale 
private investment in MSME finance.

Germany became 
the first donor to the Frontier Opportunities Fund, a 
novel financing vehicle that uses concessional first-loss 
capital to improve risk-return profiles and catalyze 
equity investment and philanthropic co-investments 
in high-impact climate projects across developing and 
emerging markets. IFC advisory and upstream trust funds complement the 
World Bank’s public sector work by helping to de-risk 
projects, develop investable opportunities, and support 
reforms that attract private capital into markets where 
it might otherwise remain on the sidelines.

These 
trust-funded activities bridge public sector reforms and 
private sector investment. In fiscal 2026, $178 million 
of development partner funding was spent on advisory 
services and upstream activities. Donor trust funds 
accounted for 43 percent of IFC’s total upstream and 
advisory resources, supporting shared World Bank 
Group priorities, including the jobs agenda and private 
capital mobilization.

IFC’s upstream work helped enable 
$23.6 billion in long-term financing for private sector 
projects — more than one-quarter of all long-term 
financing committed by IFC and its partners during 
the year. In fiscal 2026, IFC’s trust-funded upstream and advisory 
work advanced job-creating projects in high-impact 
sectors such as infrastructure, agribusiness, and 
value-added manufacturing, including in fragile and 
conflict-affected situations.

In Bangladesh, Australia 
supported the Laldia Container Terminal public-private 
partnership (PPP) through IFC’s South Asia Regional 
Infrastructure and Connectivity trust fund. IFC’s PPP 
transaction advisory work helped structure the project 
and mobilized more than $760 million in private 
investment. The project is expected to generate more 
than 3,000 jobs, including 500-700 direct positions at 
the terminal, plus significant indirect employment in 
logistics and manufacturing.

In the Democratic Republic 
of the Congo, the United Kingdom, through a new trust 
fund contribution, supported IFC’s Scaling Finance for 
Agribusinesses program, which aims to create jobs and 
improve livelihoods by expanding access to finance, 
agricultural equipment, and business opportunities 
for women entrepreneurs, smallholder farmers, and 
agricultural small businesses.

In Ukraine, the Japan-
IFC Comprehensive Trust Fund is supporting the 
development of the NovaSklo Greenfield project, which 
aims to establish the country’s first domestic float-
glass manufacturing facility through feasibility, risk,

reviews; financial modeling; and prospective investor 
engagement. Once operational, it is expected to 
support Ukraine’s reconstruction by reducing reliance 
on imports, creating more than 300 direct jobs, and 
generating additional employment across related 
value chains.

DE-RISKING THROUGH GUARANTEES 
MIGA completes the World Bank Group’s integrated 
approach by using trust funds to provide guarantee 
instruments that de-risk investments for both public 
and private sector projects. Trust funds, including the 
Renewable Energy Catalyst Trust Fund, the West Bank 
and Gaza Trust Fund, and the Support for Ukraine’s 
Reconstruction and Economy Trust Fund, share 
guarantee exposure on individual projects via first-loss 
layers and reinsurance.

These instruments enable MIGA 
to bridge the World Bank’s public sector work and IFC’s 
private sector investments by guaranteeing higher-risk 
projects and increasing investor confidence, particularly 
in fragile and conflict-affected settings, while advancing 
job creation and women’s economic empowerment. The Fund for Advancing Sustainability complements 
these efforts by strengthening environmental, social, 
and gender practices and broadening access to 
guarantees for small businesses in low-income 
and fragile countries.

FINANCIAL INTERMEDIARY FUNDS 
Financial intermediary funds (FIFs) represent large, 
distinct, multi-partner financing arrangements, for 
which the World Bank provides administrative support. They enable the international community to pool 
and coordinate funding from many sources to tackle 
specific development challenges, such as disease, 
food security, and other systemic changes. FIFs are 
independently governed, and the World Bank Group 
has no decision-making authority.

Instead, FIFs rely on 
the World Bank to provide financial and other services 
to facilitate their funding efforts and decisions. The 
World Bank serves as trustee for 27 FIFs. At the end of 
fiscal 2026, $45.2 billion was held in trust in the form 
of cash, investments, and promissory notes for FIFs. Seventeen FIFs have also selected the World Bank to 
host their secretariats, and 19 FIFs use World Bank 
Group institutions as their implementing entities. For more information, visit https://www. worldbank.org/en/about/unit/pim.

WORLD BANK 
(IBRD/IDA)
The World Bank comprises two institutions: the International Bank for Reconstruction and 
Development (IBRD) and the International Development Association (IDA). IBRD provides financial 
products and policy advice to help countries reduce poverty and extend the benefits of sustainable 
growth to all their people. IDA provides grants and concessional loans to low-income countries. 49

AND FINANCIAL MODEL 
IBRD finances its loans through its own equity and by 
borrowing in the capital markets via the issuance of 
IBRD bonds to fund development projects in member 
countries.

IBRD is rated triple-A by both Moody’s and 
Standard & Poor’s, and investors view its bonds as high-
quality and liquid securities. IBRD’s funding approach 
continues to aim to achieve the best long-term value 
for borrowing members on a sustainable basis. IBRD’s 
ability to channel the funds it raises in international 
capital markets to developing member countries is 
important in achieving its goals. IBRD’s approach has enabled it to borrow at favorable 
market terms and pass the savings on to its borrowing 
members.

Funds not immediately deployed for lending 
are held in IBRD’s investment portfolio to provide 
liquidity for its operations. In fiscal 2026, IBRD raised 
nearly $50 billion by issuing medium- and long-term 
bonds in a variety of currencies. As a cooperative institution, IBRD does not seek to 
maximize profit but rather to earn enough income to 
ensure the long-term financial capacity necessary to 
sustain its development activities.

Allocable net income 
in fiscal 2026 was $2.3 billion, and out of this, the 
Executive Directors approved the allocation of 
$1.1 billion to the General Reserve, and recommended 
to the Board of Governors an allocation of $750 million 
to IDA and $500 million to Surplus. Further, the Board 
recommended to IBRD’s Board of Governors the 
following transfers out of Surplus: $300 million to the 
IBRD Trust Fund for Gaza and West Bank, $100 million 
to the Grant Facility for Project Preparation, and 
$100 million to the IBRD Surplus-Funded Livable Planet 
Fund.

As part of its lending, borrowing, and investment 
activities, IBRD is exposed to market, counterparty, 
country credit, and operational risks. The World Bank Group’s Chief Risk Officer (CRO) 
leads the risk oversight function covering financial, 
operational, model, and environmental and social 
risks. The CRO also supports the institutional decision-
making process through dedicated risk committees 
that cover financial, operational, and franchise risks. In addition, IBRD has implemented a strong risk 
management framework to support management in 
its oversight functions.

The framework is designed to 
enable and support IBRD in achieving its goals in a 
financially sustainable manner. One summary measure 
of IBRD’s risk profile is equity-to-loans ratio, which 
is closely managed in line with its financial and risk 
outlook. As of June 30, 2026, this ratio was 21.6 percent, 
and IBRD’s cumulative subscribed capital totaled 
$332.5 billion, including $23.6 billion in paid-in capital. 53

The World Bank (IBRD/IDA) offers a variety of financing 
instruments and approaches to help countries achieve 
their development goals.

These include:
• Investment Project Financing, which helps build 
physical and social infrastructure and develop 
institutional capacity;
• Development Policy Financing, which supports 
policy and institutional reforms, including through 
policy-based guarantees; and
• Program-for-Results Financing, which links the 
disbursement of funds to the achievement of 
predefined results.

In fiscal 2026, we approved 58 Development 
Policy Financing operations, totaling $24.2 billion; 
62 Program-for-Results operations, of which 13 were 
additional financing, totaling $15.8 billion; and 
251 Investment Project Financing operations, of which 
81 were additional financing, totaling $40.9 billion. Our own-account climate co-benefits reached 
$48 billion in fiscal 2026, representing 44 percent of 
total World Bank commitments, including 30 percent 
for Development Policy Financing, 38 percent for 
Program-for-Results, and 54 percent for Investment 
Project Financing.

We also mobilized a record 
$48 billion in climate co-benefits through private 
sector financing, bringing the combined total to nearly 
$96 billion, up 21 percent from fiscal 2025. Our Multiphase Programmatic Approach (MPA) 
enables countries to structure long, large, or complex 
engagements as a set of smaller, complementary 
Investment Project Financing and Program-for-Results 
operations within a single program.

This approach facilitates both vertical programs, 
which involve in-depth, sustained engagement within 
a single country, and horizontal programs, which 
encompass multiple countries, states within a country, 
or subnational entities. In fiscal 2026, the World Bank 
approved 33 new programs totaling $25.1 billion in 
financing, comprising 15 vertical programs ($8.2 billion) 
and 18 horizontal programs ($16.9 billion). Total MPA 
project approvals comprised 95 projects totaling 
$17.7 billion, including nine additional financing 
projects totaling $1.0 billion.

As of June 2026, a total of 80 countries have 
implemented at least one instrument from the Crisis 
Preparedness and Response Toolkit. With those 
instruments, countries have pre-arranged contingent 
resources and catastrophe bonds/insurance, allowing

BUILDING NEW AND IMPROVED PLATFORMS 
FOR MOBILIZING PRIVATE CAPITAL 
Large institutional investors, such as pension funds, 
insurance companies, and asset managers, typically 
allocate capital through standardized asset classes 
and systematic distribution rather than for individual 
transactions. IFC’s originate-to-distribute business 
model is designed to meet those needs by creating 
diversified packages of assets — across multiple 
projects and markets — that are structured in a 
form that is recognizable and can be in some cases 
independently rated.

The originate-to-distribute 
pathway includes existing mobilization products with 
significant investor engagement, such as B loans, while 
broadening IFC’s approach to investor participation 
through more systematic and standardized channels of 
distribution, including securitization. In September 2025, IFC launched the Emerging Markets 
Securitization Program (EMSP), a significant step 
forward in our originate-to-distribute program. EMSP 
recycles IFC’s loans into packaged securities in which 
investors such as asset managers, pension funds, and 
insurance companies can invest.

The $510 million 
transaction was listed on the London Stock Exchange, 
giving visibility, pricing transparency, liquidity, and 
the prospect of secondary trading. The second 
transaction under the EMSP was completed in June 
2026, demonstrating its ability to replicate and scale. These transactions benefited from a catalytic equity 
co-investment from the UK Government’s Mobilist 
Program alongside IFC. IFC further expanded its originate-to-distribute 
program in fiscal 2026 with the inaugural Trade Finance 
Synthetic Securitization (TFSS).

The TFSS is composed 
of $500 million trade assets originated under IFC’s 
Global Trade Finance Program, which has more than 
half its portfolio in low-income and fragile and conflict-
affected states. The transaction’s private capital 
mobilization ratio is up to 1:19, meaning for every 
dollar of risk retained by IFC, up to $19 are taken 
up by private investors. The originate-to-distribute model that underpins 
the EMSP and TFSS can be standardized and scaled, 
providing an efficient means to draw substantially 
more private capital into emerging markets.

IFC also continued to build upon proven platforms for 
mobilizing private capital at scale. One of the most 
effective is the Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program 
(MCPP), a portfolio syndications platform through 
which investors can gain exposure to a diverse mix of 
loans to private sector borrowers in emerging markets. In fiscal 2026, the MCPP mobilized $6 billion from 19 
global insurers to support lending to financial 
institutions in emerging markets.

By sharing the credit 
risk on a portion of IFC’s loan portfolio, the program 
frees up balance sheet capacity and is expected to 
support up to $10 billion in new IFC financing to 
small- and medium-sized enterprises. It is IFC’s largest 
mobilization under a single agreement. ADDRESSING THE SHORTAGE OF EQUITY 
IN EMERGING MARKET FIRMS 
Equity is the scarcest form of financing in emerging 
markets and the foundation for sustainable business 
growth. IFC is working to increase its own equity 
investments while developing new ways to bring equity 
from other investors into developing economies.

IFC has expanded its capacity to deploy junior equity 
by investing $100 million of its net income to seed 
the Frontier Opportunities Fund. The fund allows IFC 
to take on more complex risk positions and crowd 
in private capital, including senior equity, to unlock 
investments in the most challenging markets. Eight 
projects have been Board-approved. As of June 30, 
2026, an additional $100 million has been allocated 
to the Frontier Opportunities Fund, allowing IFC to 
meet the burgeoning pipeline of projects.

The portfolio 
covers a wide range of sectors, including carbon 
finance, energy access and transition, green hydrogen, 
and industrial transformation. EXTENDING MORE CAPITAL AND 
SUPPORT TO MSMEs 
Reaching micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises 
is central to the jobs challenge. These businesses are 
the largest employers in developing economies, yet 
they are often the hardest to serve.

IFC is expanding 
its reach through digital platforms, supply chain 
integration, and tailored financing — going beyond 
financial institutions to connect entrepreneurs more 
directly to capital and markets. Integrating into supply chains can propel growth for 
smaller enterprises. To that end, a new risk-sharing 
facility launched in fiscal 2026 with Standard Chartered 
is designed to strengthen supply chains for businesses 
across Africa.

The partnership introduces supply 
chain finance solutions in eight markets: Côte d’Ivoire, 
Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, 
and Zambia. Over the next three years, it is projected 
to enable about $1.9 billion in supply chain finance 
transactions, supporting more than 500 suppliers in 
both domestic and global value chains. CREATING MARKETS IN FRAGILE AND 
CONFLICT-AFFECTED COUNTRIES 
Fragile, conflict-affected, and violence-affected 
(FCV) countries are where the private sector gap is 
widest and the need for jobs most urgent.

By 2030, 
nearly 60 percent of the world’s extreme poor will 
live in FCV countries. The World Bank Group’s FCV 
Strategy, launched in fiscal 2026, is the institution’s 
five-year response, with IFC leading on efforts to 
mobilize private investment in the markets where 
it is most scarce. IFC is the largest development finance institution in 
fragile and conflict-affected situations and, in line with 
the broader World Bank Group strategy, IFC’s approach 
is calibrated to context.

In improving markets, IFC takes

A persistent barrier to private investment in emerging 
markets is the mismatch between perceived and actual 
risk.

The Global Emerging Markets Risk Database 
(GEMs) Consortium — the largest source of credit 
risk data for investments in emerging markets and 
developing economies — addresses this directly by 
providing hard data that allows investors and rating 
agencies to assess risk more accurately and price 
it more fairly. As confidence in emerging market 
asset quality grows, so does the potential to attract 
institutional capital at scale.

The Consortium was created in 2009 on the initiative 
of the European Investment Bank and IFC and has 
evolved into a community of practice that develops 
common approaches and data methodologies to 
record default and recovery frequencies for the 
member multilateral development banks and 
development finance institutions. In fiscal 2026, GEMs released three updated reports: 
Default and Recovery Statistics: Private Lending 1994–
2024; Default and Recovery Statistics: Public Lending 
1994–2024; and Default and Recovery Statistics: Sovereign 
and Sovereign-guaranteed Lending 1984–2024.

These 
offer new, more granular statistics, providing investors 
and other GEMs users with greater insights and 
more information. MEASURING WHAT MATTERS IN 
DEVELOPMENT IMPACT 
Development impact is a core component of IFC’s 
mandate. IFC prioritizes rigorous measurement, 
monitoring, and evaluation of the development impact 
of its investment and advisory operations.

When making investment decisions, IFC systematically 
weighs development impact alongside financial 
returns, risks, and alignment with strategic objectives 
and priorities, with a particular focus on fostering 
opportunities for underserved populations in 
emerging and underdeveloped markets.

To that end, 
IFC developed its impact management tool — the 
Anticipated Impact Measurement and Monitoring 
(AIMM) system.8 For the past eight years, IFC has 
been assessing the development impact of all our 
investments and assigning each an impact rating 
(Excellent, Good, Satisfactory, Low) to inform 
investment decisions.

The AIMM ratings for investment projects at entry have 
improved as IFC has increasingly focused more on high-
impact areas such as low-income countries, climate, 
small businesses, and other thematic priorities such as 
working with underserved and vulnerable populations. In fiscal 2026, IFC committed 341 AIMM-assessed 
investment projects with 96 percent of them rated 
Good or Excellent — one percentage point higher than 
the previous fiscal year.

IFC also monitors active projects in the portfolio and 
tracks key development impact indicators to allow 
us to take corrective action when projects are off 
track. In fiscal 2026, 65 percent of the 1,570 projects 
in the AIMM portfolio were rated Good or Excellent, 
compared to 62 percent in fiscal 2025. We also conduct 
comprehensive assessment of project development 
impact at the end of the project’s implementation 
period.

In fiscal 2026, 45 percent of the 168 projects 
that completed their implementation in that year were 
rated Good or Excellent, representing 49 percent of 
the corresponding commitment volume. Changes 
in impact ratings during implementation have been 
associated primarily with country and macroeconomic 
factors, with client, and market or industry factors also 
playing a role.

The development impact of all our investments 
is monitored using outcome indicators identified 
for each project at the time of approval, including 
indicators that track their impact on their ultimate 
expected beneficiaries.

For example, we track the 
number and volume of loans provided by financial 
intermediaries to small businesses; the number 
of farmers that benefit from improved access to 
inputs, product markets, finance, or better farming 
practices; the number of patients that receive health 
services; the number of students that receive access 
to education; the growth in access to infrastructure 
services; and the greenhouse gas emissions that are 
avoided thanks to new technologies.

The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), home of the World Bank Group Guarantee 
Platform, provides guarantees to facilitate the flow of foreign investment in developing countries, 
enabling the private sector to create jobs. Our mandate is to encourage investment into developing 
member countries by providing non-commercial risk guarantees (political risk insurance, credit 
enhancement products, and trade finance guarantees) to investors and lenders.

In fiscal 2026, MIGA marked a major milestone by 
surpassing $100 billion in cumulative guarantees 
issued since its founding in 1988. With just $366 million 
of paid-in capital from member countries, MIGA has 
steadily pursued its stated mission for nearly four 
decades by providing guarantees to private investors. This paves the way for private funds to flow to emerging 
and developing economies, enabling job creation.

In its second year, fiscal 2026, the World Bank Group 
Guarantee Platform issued $17.9 billion in guarantees 
to 110 projects in 32 countries, an increase of 
46 percent over fiscal 2025. Of this, MIGA issued a 
record $10.6 billion in new guarantees across 60 
projects. Through these projects, MIGA encouraged 
private investment to facilitate economic development 
in host countries by helping clients manage and 
mitigate non-commercial risks.

The majority of projects 
advanced at least one of MIGA’s strategic priorities: 38 
projects were climate finance initiatives, 20 projects 
were in IDA–eligible countries, and 10 projects were in 
fragile and conflict-affected situations.

As a result, the fiscal 2026 issuances are expected to: 
• Mobilize $11 billion in private capital 
• Provide 300,000 people and businesses with 
access to finance 
• Strengthen food and nutrition security for 
4 million people 
• Enable 2.7 gigawatts in renewable energy capacity
• Avoid more than 4.7 million metric tons of 
greenhouse gas emissions annually 
An institution of the World Bank Group, MIGA is 
committed to creating strong development impact 
and supporting projects that are economically, 
environmentally, and socially sustainable.

leverage its investment guarantee capacity, manage 
its portfolio risk profile, and foster the growth of the 
private political risk insurance market.

benefits have accrued both to MIGA’s investors, who 
have gained access to higher levels of coverage for 
projects in developing countries, and to host countries, 
which have benefited from much higher levels of 
productive foreign investment. MIGA ceded $7.5 billion of new business to the

in using reinsurance is to support its growth while 
managing portfolio concentration and ensuring 
efficient capital utilization.

The increased use of 
reinsurance is also in line with the World Bank Group 
goal of leveraging the private sector into financing 
development, as well as with MIGA’s strategy of 
preserving capital to fund future growth, primarily 
in priority areas. As of June 30, 2026, $28.7 billion or

MIGA’S TOTAL ISSUANCE OVER $100 BILLION 
MIGA was established as a member of the World Bank 
Group by an international convention in April 1988, 
with 29 original member countries sharing the goal 
of accelerating the flow of private investment into 
developing countries by insuring against political risks. Its mission, “To promote foreign direct investment into 
developing countries to support economic growth, 
reduce poverty, and improve people’s lives,” 
is consistent with the World Bank Group’s goals.

This fiscal year, MIGA surpassed $100 billion in 
guarantees issued since its founding. With just 
$366 million of paid-in capital from member countries, 
MIGA has steadily pursued that mission for nearly four 
decades by providing guarantees to private investors, 
paving the way for private funds to flow to emerging 
and developing economies, enabling job creation. A framework agreement for a portfolio of guarantees 
of up to $1.5 billion, issued in March to AMEA Power 
Limited, pushed MIGA’s cumulative guarantee issuance 
past the $100 billion mark, a major milestone for 
the institution.

11TH ANNUAL MIGA GENDER 
LEADERSHIP AWARD 
This fiscal year marked the 11th year of the MIGA 
Gender Leadership Award, which recognizes senior 
managers with a proven track record of furthering the 
cause of women’s advancement and gender equality 
in business while contributing to the mission of the 
World Bank Group to end extreme poverty and boost 
prosperity on a livable planet. The award is presented 
annually to mark International Women’s Day. This year’s award recipient was Katarina Zdraljevic, 
Head of Group Sustainability at ProCredit Holding 
of Germany. Ms.

Zdraljevic has spent 14 years in 
development finance with the ProCredit Group, 
focusing on decarbonization, sustainable agriculture, 
and green finance for small businesses in Latin America, 
Southeastern Europe, and Eastern Europe. She also 
serves on the board of ProCredit Bank Ecuador. Ms. Zdraljevic has been a strong advocate for inclusive 
finance and gender equality.

She led the adoption of 
MIGA’s Gender Action Plan for ProCredit, including the 
development and implementation of a Board-approved 
gender strategy that integrates internal practices and 
client-facing lending, including gender training at all 
levels. More than 20 percent of ProCredit’s small-
business loans support firms that are at least 50 
percent owned or led by women. ProCredit projects 
have supported some 193,000 jobs, with 42 percent 
of them held by women. Ms. Zdraljevic also continues 
to participate in external gender forums such as the 
Financial Alliance for Women.

GUARANTEEING FINANCIAL 
STABILITY IN PANAMA 
When Panama faced serious fiscal strain in 2025, the 
World Bank Group responded with an unprecedented 
approach by combining IBRD and MIGA guarantees in 
a jointly structured policy-based financing operation.

Building on lessons from a similar operation in Côte 
d’Ivoire, teams designed a layered structure pairing 
a $500 million IBRD Development Policy Loan with 
$1.4 billion in commercial financing covered by 
two guarantees: a $600 million IBRD Policy-Based 
Guarantee for first-loss coverage, and a MIGA Non-
Honoring of Sovereign Financial Obligations guarantee 
for second-loss coverage. This approach, resulting in approximately $1.9 billion 
in financing, was approved simultaneously by 
both institutions’ boards, moving from approval to 
disbursement in about a month.

Anchored in a strong, government-led reform program, 
the operation extended maturities, lowered costs, and 
signaled market confidence in Panama’s fiscal path. It serves as a model for other countries facing similar 
financial pressures. TRANSFORMING RAIL AND 
CONNECTIVITY ALONG THE TRANS- 
CASPIAN TRANSPORT CORRIDOR 
The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, also known as 
the Middle Corridor, is a network of road, rail, and sea 
routes linking East Asian and European markets via 
Central Asia, the Caucasus, and Türkiye.

The World Bank Group is unlocking the Corridor’s 
potential to become an engine of jobs and economic 
growth by mobilizing more than $8.3 billion in 
public and private financing for enhanced rail and 
multimodal connectivity. In fiscal 2026, we achieved milestones in two countries 
along the Corridor: In Kazakhstan, a budding transport 
hub, the World Bank approved an $846 million 
guarantee to mobilize $1.4 billion in public and private 
financing for the new Mointy–Kyzylzhar railway line.

IFC 
mobilized $250 million in private finance for the Almaty 
Railway Bypass, with a $113 million MIGA guarantee to 
mitigate risks. In Türkiye, the World Bank is providing a 
$2 billion loan for the Istanbul North Rail Crossing and 
leading six multilateral development banks to mobilize 
$6.3 billion in public financing for the project. The development of the Corridor is projected to 
create jobs in all host countries, boosting long-term 
employment by more than 3 percent in Kazakhstan, 
the Kyrgyz Republic, and Armenia, and by more than 
4 percent in Türkiye.

With this portfolio of projects 
along the Corridor, and those to follow, the World Bank 
Group is fueling job creation, regional integration, and 
economic development. EXPANDING TRADE FINANCE 
IN EMERGING MARKETS 
Trade finance gaps are widening across emerging 
markets as global risk appetite tightens, leaving state-
owned banks, which are often critical for importing 
essential goods, struggling to access affordable 
financing.

In response, MIGA partnered with Deutsche 
Bank to launch a €1 billion trade finance guarantee 
platform, MIGA’s first stand-alone wholesale 
arrangement with a global commercial bank. Under the platform, MIGA guarantees protect Deutsche 
Bank against non-payment risk in trade transactions 
involving eligible state-owned banks, helping unlock 
financing that supports imports and underserved 
client segments. The platform sets targets to direct a 
meaningful share of enabled volume toward priority 
areas, including IDA and fragile countries, small 
businesses, agriculture, health, and water.

By pairing MIGA’s risk mitigation capacity with Deutsche 
Bank’s global trade finance network, the platform is 
designed to sustain and expand financing availability 
precisely where gaps are growing fastest. Building on Deutsche Bank’s engagement with 
the World Bank Group since 1959, this innovative 
partnership marks a significant step in mobilizing 
private capital as a multiplier for development finance. 79

The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) supports cross-border 
investment by offering an independent, specialized forum for the resolution of disputes. Effective, 
impartial dispute resolution strengthens confidence among investors and States and enhances 
predictability — core pillars of a favorable investment landscape. ICSID is a unique institution, created by the Convention 
on the Settlement of Investment Disputes between 
States and Nationals of Other States.

This multilateral 
agreement, also known as the ICSID Convention, was 
formulated in 1965 by the Executive Directors of the 
World Bank. ICSID is essential to the World Bank Group’s work to 
accelerate job creation at scale, a strategy focused on 
investing in the physical and human infrastructure 
that people and businesses need to thrive, supporting 
business-enabling environments, and mobilizing 
private capital.

By providing an effective, impartial forum for resolving 
international investment disputes, ICSID mitigates 
perceived risk and encourages the mobilization of 
private capital across borders. The availability of ICSID 
to investors and States fosters trust and predictability, 
helping create investment environments that drive 
economic growth and job creation.

At the core of this work are ICSID’s dispute 
administration services, which cover a range of 
procedures including arbitration, conciliation, 
mediation, and fact-finding for disputes arising from 
investment contracts, international treaties, and 
domestic investment laws. ICSID’s rules and procedures 
are widely regarded as the gold standard for 
investment dispute settlement, offering a stable and 
predictable legal framework that balances the interests 
of both States and investors and has been modernized 
over time to reflect best practices in the field.

ICSID also supports the development of international 
investment law and dispute settlement by producing 
and sharing knowledge, building capacity, and 
engaging with Member States and other stakeholders 
on investment dispute prevention, management, 
and settlement. Fiscal 2026 saw meaningful progress across all these 
areas, as ICSID advanced its priorities to deepen 
engagement and knowledge, expand mediation and 
amicable settlement, and uphold the highest standards 
in case management.

ICSID
On March 6, 2026, President Nasry Juan Asfura of Honduras signed the ICSID 
Convention in Washington, D.C., making Honduras the 166th Signatory State to the 
Convention. ICSID Membership has steadily expanded since the ICSID Convention 
opened for signature in 1965. By the early 2000s, 149 States had signed the ICSID 
Convention, and 132 of those had ratified it. By June 30, 2026, the number of signatories 
had increased to 166 States, with 158 of them becoming Contracting States.

ICSID membership is considered a positive factor in MIGA’s risk assessment for insurance 
guarantees and the World Bank Group’s overall assessment of countries’ investment 
landscape. ICSID membership supports States’ policies to attract and retain foreign direct 
investment to create more job opportunities and economic growth. It signals States’ 
openness to resolving disputes through arbitration, conciliation, and mediation in a 
trusted forum established under an international convention. There is no cost to join or 
maintain membership in ICSID.

MEMBERSHIP UPDATES AND BENEFITS
REACHING FURTHER, WORKING CLOSER 
ICSID continued to deepen its worldwide engagement 
in fiscal 2026. Staff participated in over 180 activities, 
the most in a single year to date, across 60 cities as part 
of a robust outreach and capacity-building program. Delivered in person and remotely in the Centre’s 
three official languages (English, Spanish, and French), 
as well as in Italian and Japanese, these activities 
reached officials from over 90 States, along with legal 
practitioners, students, and representatives of regional 
and local institutions.

Collaboration with sister institutions also grew stronger, 
reinforcing a One World Bank Group approach in 
practice. The Centre deepened ties with country 
offices through targeted training sessions and worked 
alongside World Bank Group legal teams to engage 
Attorneys General and Ministers of Justice at high-
level forums on business-enabling environments and 
public-private partnerships. Collaboration with IFC and 
MIGA is ongoing, focused on sharing knowledge about 
investor-State dispute prevention and resolution with 
their clients.

This partnership also extended to joint 
analytical and operational work: World Bank Group 
research is examining the impact of ICSID membership 
on bilateral foreign direct investment flows; the 
Business Ready (B-READY) team integrated ICSID-
related questions into its 2026 data collection cycle; 
and ICSID contributed to World Bank Group reports on 
dispute resolution, supported the development of legal 
frameworks for carbon markets, and co-organized a 
conference on investment arbitration.

ICSID also remains actively engaged in multilateral 
efforts to modernize investor-State dispute settlement 
(ISDS) mechanisms. In fiscal 2026, the Centre 
participated in five sessions of the United Nations 
Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) 
Working Group III, contributing substantively to 
State-led reform discussions, including by submitting 
comments on the feasibility of modifying the ICSID 
Convention to allow awards to be reviewed by a 
permanent appellate tribunal.

ICSID also deepened 
its engagement with the International Institute for the 
Unification of Private Law (UNIDROIT) in support of 
efforts to modernize and harmonize investor-State 
investment contracts. EXPANDING GLOBAL PRESENCE

SHARING KNOWLEDGE, SUPPORTING 
PRACTITIONERS AND POLICYMAKERS 
As part of the Knowledge Bank, ICSID produces and 
shares knowledge that actively contributes to the 
development and modernization of international 
investment law and dispute settlement. In fiscal 2026, ICSID published its first in-depth study on 
contract-based investment dispute resolution, drawing 
on an analysis of 175 cases registered under the ICSID 
Convention and Additional Facility.

The background 
paper examines how contract-based dispute resolution 
has worked in practice at ICSID, serving as both an 
analytical guide and practical reference for investors, 
States, and State entities. Key findings show that 
contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more time-
efficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months 
from registration to conclusion compared to 47, and 
settle or discontinue at a higher rate, 43 percent versus 
34 percent. The paper is accompanied by a special 
issue of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics featuring data on 
contract-based cases.

A revised set of Model Clauses for Contracts was also 
released, providing ready-to-use drafting language 
for contracts between foreign investors and States or 
Regional Economic Integration Organizations, including 
State subdivisions and agencies, that seek to submit 
disputes to ICSID. Updated for the first time since 
1993, the Model Clauses cover arbitration, conciliation, 
mediation, and fact-finding at ICSID, offering practical 
templates that parties can adapt to their specific needs. Three issues of the ICSID Review – Foreign Investment Law 
Journal were published during the year.

A specialized, 
peer-reviewed publication produced in collaboration 
with Oxford University Press, the journal offers analysis 
of legal developments, significant cases, and practical 
issues in foreign investment law and international 
dispute settlement. One issue was a special 
edition on the energy transition, exploring diverse 
perspectives on its implications for investment law. Two issues of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics were also 
released.

ICSID administers investment disputes arising from 
contracts, treaties, or laws when agreed upon by the 
parties involved.

Disputes are decided by an arbitral 
tribunal or a conciliation commission, whose members 
are typically appointed by the parties from among 
international jurists worldwide. The Centre also offers 
mediation and fact-finding procedures, and provides 
administrative services for arbitrations conducted
